q: Given an UNSORTED array and a target, return the indexes of two numbers that add up to the target. You must return the original indexes.
options: Hash map that remembers the numbers already seen
Sort the array and use two pointers
why: Sorting would lose the original indexes. A hash map lets you ask "have I already seen target - x?" in O(1), giving O(n) overall.

q: A SORTED array is given. Find two numbers that add up to a target using O(1) extra space.
options: Two pointers moving in from both ends
why: In a sorted array a sum that is too small means the left pointer must move right, and too big means the right pointer must move left. O(n) time, O(1) space.

q: Find the length of the longest substring of a string that has no repeated characters.
options: Sliding window that grows and shrinks
Binary search on the length only
why: The answer is a contiguous part, and a window can grow on the right and shrink on the left whenever a repeat appears. One pass, O(n).

q: A fixed array is queried thousands of times: "what is the sum of the elements from index l to r?" Each query must be O(1).
options: Prefix sums built once in O(n)
why: prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] answers any range sum with one subtraction after a single O(n) setup.

q: Koko must eat all banana piles within h hours. Find the MINIMUM eating speed k (bananas per hour) that makes it possible.
options: Greedy: sort the piles and eat the biggest first
Binary search on the answer k
why: If speed k works, every faster speed works too, so "can she finish at speed k?" flips from no to yes once. Binary search the speed, checking each guess in O(n).

q: For every day in a list of temperatures, find how many days you must wait until a warmer temperature.
why: Keep a stack of days still waiting for a warmer day. A warmer day pops everything colder, and each day is pushed and popped once: O(n).

q: Given a list of meeting time ranges, merge all the ranges that overlap.
options: Sort by start time, then merge neighbours
why: After sorting by start, overlap only needs a comparison with the last merged range: start <= last end.

q: In a grid maze every move costs 1 step. Find the minimum number of steps from the start cell to the exit.
options: Depth-first search that tries every path
why: BFS explores level by level, so the first time it reaches the exit it has used the fewest steps (all moves cost the same).

q: Count the number of islands (groups of connected 1s) in a grid of 0s and 1s.
options: Flood-fill with DFS from each unvisited 1
why: Each time you find an unvisited 1 you have found a new island; DFS marks every cell of it so it is not counted twice.

q: Compute the diameter (longest path between any two nodes) of a binary tree.
options: Recursion that combines the heights of the left and right subtrees
why: At each node the longest path through it is left height + right height. Post-order recursion returns the height up and records the best path.

q: Courses have prerequisites. Return an order in which all courses can be taken, or report that it is impossible.
why: Prerequisites form a directed graph. Repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites; if you cannot take them all there is a cycle.

q: Edges are added one by one to an undirected graph. Find the edge that first creates a cycle.
options: Binary search on the edge number
why: Union-find merges groups and tells you in almost O(1) whether two nodes are already connected; an edge between connected nodes closes a cycle.

q: Roads between cities have different non-negative lengths. Find the shortest route from city A to every other city.
why: BFS only counts edges. With different weights you always expand the nearest unfinished city, which a min-heap gives you: Dijkstra.

q: Generate all subsets of a list, or all valid combinations of n pairs of parentheses.
why: The answer is every valid arrangement, so you build it one decision at a time, recurse, and undo the decision to try the next.

q: Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping activities that one person can attend.
options: Greedy: sort by end time and take whatever fits
why: Taking the activity that finishes earliest leaves the most room for the rest, and an exchange argument shows it never hurts.

q: Find the fewest coins that make a given amount, with arbitrary denominations such as 1, 3 and 4 for the amount 6.
options: Greedy: always take the largest coin
why: Greedy gives 4+1+1 (3 coins) but 3+3 (2 coins) is better. The best answer for amount a is 1 + the best answer for a - c over all coins c, which DP builds from small amounts up.

q: From a huge stream of words, return the k most frequent in about O(n log k) time.
options: Sort the whole stream every time
why: Keep a heap holding the best k seen so far. A newcomer only replaces the weakest of them, so each item costs O(log k).

q: Store a dictionary of words and quickly list every word that starts with a given prefix (autocomplete).
options: Sorted array and binary search on every query
why: A trie follows one letter at a time, so a prefix lookup costs O(length of the prefix) however many words are stored.

q: Decide whether a linked list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra memory.
options: Store every visited node in a hash set
why: A fast pointer (2 steps) laps a slow one (1 step) inside a loop, so they meet. The hash set also works but costs O(n) memory, which the question rules out.

q: Every number in an array appears twice except one. Find it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
why: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, so the pairs cancel and the single number is left. The hash map works in O(n) but uses O(n) space.

q: Support adding numbers one at a time and reading the median of everything added so far.
options: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half
Sort the whole list after every insert
why: The two heaps hold the halves around the middle; the median sits on their tops, so insertion is O(log n) and the median is O(1).
